transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi. Thank you. Um, so, honestly, what really made me finally make the call to come in is... well, it’s mostly work stuff. I’m an advertising sales agent, and a lot of the job is great, I love talking to clients, but we have these massive, incredibly long sales strategy meetings. Like, sometimes they stretch on for hours and hours. And I know I’m supposed to just stay seated—everyone else is just sitting there, perfectly fine, looking at the revenue projections and taking notes—but I just keep getting up. 

Over and over. And I know it looks bad, I know I need to just stay in my chair, but I’ll find literally any excuse to get out of it. I'll get up to refill my water bottle, and then I'll drink it really fast just so I have a reason to go get more water twenty minutes later. Or I’ll tell myself I need to check if an agenda finished printing, and I’ll just sort of pace by the printer for a minute or two before I force myself to go back in. 

My boss actually gave me this look the other day because I was up and down so much, and it was just really embarrassing. It’s just... I don't know, it’s frustrating because I’m thirty years old, I have a degree, I should be able to just sit through a standard corporate meeting, right? But I just keep leaving my seat even when I absolutely know I shouldn't be. So, yeah, that's the main thing.
Do you find yourself feeling restless or needing to get up and move around in other situations, outside of these long meetings?

Um, well, outside of the meetings? I mean, I guess... not really? Like, obviously those meetings are the worst part, they're just so agonizingly long and dry. But in other situations, I don't know, I don't think I really have that same problem. Like, when I'm at home, I'm usually pretty okay. I mean, I might get up to grab a snack or check my phone or something, but it's not like I feel this intense, overwhelming urge to just escape my chair like I do at work. 

And even at work, if I'm just at my desk, you know, making calls or sending emails, I'm fine. I can sit there and do my thing. It's really just those specific, structured situations where I'm expected to be completely still and focused for hours on end. I don't know, maybe it's just the environment? Like, the fluorescent lights and the boring PowerPoint presentations and the fact that I can't really contribute much to the conversation, so I just feel like I'm trapped there. So, yeah, I wouldn't say I'm restless all the time or anything. It's just... those meetings. They're just the worst.
Do you feel anxious or uneasy in other structured or formal situations, like when you're in a client meeting or a presentation?

Um, anxious or uneasy? Honestly, no, not really. I mean, client meetings are actually the part of the job I really love. When I'm pitching a campaign or going over ad placements with a client, I'm completely in my element. I think it's because it's interactive, you know? Like, I'm talking, they're talking, we're brainstorming, we're negotiating... it's fast-paced. I don't feel that same weird, crawling need to escape my chair because my brain is actually engaged. 

And even presentations—if I'm the one presenting, I'm totally fine. I actually kind of thrive on that energy. I'll walk around the room, use my hands a lot, point at the slides... I'm moving, but it's purposeful movement, so it doesn't feel like I'm just awkwardly pacing by the printer, if that makes sense. It's really just when I'm forced to be a passive participant. Like, if I'm just an audience member in a formal setting, like those internal strategy meetings, or... oh, I guess if I go to a conference and there's a keynote speaker who just drones on and on, I might feel a little bit of that same urge to get up, but even then, I usually just sit near the back so I can slip out to the bathroom without making a scene. 

But no, I wouldn't say I feel anxious. It's not a nervous thing. It's not like my heart is racing because I'm scared or worried about what people think of me—well, except for when my boss gives me that look, obviously. But the feeling itself, the urge to get up, it's not anxiety. It's just this... physical discomfort. Like my legs just want to do something else. But yeah, in client meetings or when I'm actively doing something, I don't feel that way at all. I'm actually really good at my job when I get to just talk to people!
Do you often find your mind wandering or have difficulty focusing on tasks outside of those long meetings?

Oh, my mind wandering? Yeah, definitely. I mean, it's not just the getting up and moving around, it's also just... staying mentally present, I guess? Like, okay, take those strategy meetings I was talking about. If I'm actually trying really hard to just stay in my seat and be good, I'll be looking right at the presenter, right? Like, I'll have my eyes fixed on the screen, and I'll be nodding, and I'll think, "Okay, I am paying attention, I am absorbing this." But then, I don't know, maybe five or ten minutes go by, and suddenly I kind of snap back to reality and realize I've just been staring at the exact same PowerPoint slide for who knows how long, and I literally have absolutely no idea what the person just said. Like, none. The last point they made is just completely gone from my brain, and I've just been sitting there thinking about, like, what I'm going to make for dinner, or a weird dream I had three nights ago, or if I need to buy more laundry detergent. 

And it happens outside of meetings, too, actually. Like, if I'm reading a client brief—which is super important, obviously, because I need to know exactly what they're looking for in their ad campaign before I pitch them—I'll start reading, and the first paragraph is fine, I'm totally with it. But then I'll get to the second or third paragraph, and my eyes are still moving across the words, but my brain is just... somewhere else entirely. I'll get to the bottom of the page and realize I haven't comprehended a single sentence since the top. So then I have to go back and re-read it. And sometimes I have to re-read the same paragraph three or four times before it actually sticks. It's so frustrating because I know I need to read it, and I want to read it, but it's like my brain just decides to take a little vacation right in the middle of a sentence. So, yeah, the mind wandering is definitely a thing, it just kind of creeps up on me even when I'm really trying to focus.
Do you feel upset or irritable when you're unable to get up and move around during those long meetings?

Um, upset or irritable? No, I don't think so. I mean, I guess it depends on what you mean by irritable, but if you mean like, getting mad or snapping at people? Then no, definitely not. It's not an emotional thing for me. It's really hard to explain, but it's not like I'm sitting there feeling angry at the presenter or resentful of my boss for making me be there—well, okay, maybe a tiny bit resentful if it's a Friday afternoon and it's gorgeous outside, but I think that's just normal, right? 

But the actual feeling of needing to move, that doesn't make me cranky. Like, take last week for example. We had this massive quarterly forecasting meeting, and I got there a couple of minutes late because a client called right as I was walking out of my cubicle, so the only seat left was right in the dead center of this long conference table. I was completely squished between two of our senior account managers, totally boxed in. I knew the second I sat down that I couldn't just get up and slip out the back door to pace the hallway like I usually try to do. 

And as the meeting dragged on—and I mean, it was easily two straight hours of just pure numbers and bar charts, just mind-numbingly dry stuff—I started getting that super intense, crawling feeling in my legs. Like they just desperately needed to stretch or walk or do absolutely anything other than be bent at a ninety-degree angle. But I wasn't sitting there feeling *upset* about it. I wasn't fuming or glaring at anyone. My internal monologue was just more like, "Oh my gosh, please let this end, please let this end, I just need to stand up, I need to go get a water, I need to stretch." It was entirely just a physical discomfort thing. 

And when the meeting finally ended, I didn't snap at the account managers when they were packing up their laptops really slowly, even though I was dying to get out. I was just like, "Ope, excuse me, just gonna squeeze past you!" and then I practically sprinted to the breakroom. I'm actually a pretty positive person overall, so getting grumpy or irritable isn't really my default state anyway, unless maybe I'm super hungry and haven't had lunch yet. But just from being stuck in a chair? No, it doesn't make me irritable or upset at all. It just makes me really, really want to stand up.
Do you often fidget with your hands or feet when you're sitting still in other situations?

Um, fidgeting with my hands or feet? Let me think about that... honestly, no, not really. I mean, I know some people are like, constantly clicking pens or bouncing their knees under the desk. My coworker Sarah, for example, she sits right next to me in the bullpen and she has this habit of tapping her acrylic nails on her ceramic coffee mug all day long, which, honestly, drives me a little crazy sometimes when I'm trying to write up a client proposal and I just hear *tap tap tap tap*. But for me? No, I don't really do that kind of stuff. 

When I'm sitting, it's not my hands or my feet that are doing something. It's more like my entire body just wants to stand up. Like I said before, it's that crawling feeling in my legs, but it's not a bouncing knee thing, if that makes sense? It's a "I need to walk" thing. Like, even if I'm at home watching a movie on the couch with my boyfriend. I'm not sitting there playing with the throw pillows or twisting my rings around or tapping my toes. I'm actually pretty still. But then, you know, halfway through the movie, I'll just suddenly be like, "I'm gonna go make popcorn," or "I'm gonna go fold that basket of laundry while we watch," because I just want to be on my feet and moving my whole self. 

So yeah, my hands and feet are usually pretty quiet. I'm not a big fidgeter in that specific sense. I guess I talk with my hands a lot, like I mentioned with the pitches and presentations, but that's just being expressive, you know? That's just how I communicate. It's not the same as fidgeting when I'm supposed to be sitting still. If I'm forced to sit still in a chair, my hands are usually just resting in my lap or resting on my keyboard. I just... I really just prefer to not be sitting in the first place! So, yeah, no pen clicking or foot tapping or anything like that for me.
Do you have trouble completing tasks or chores at home because you get distracted or lose focus?

Um, chores at home? I mean, yeah, I guess sometimes I'll leave a laundry basket sitting in the hallway or whatever, but honestly, where it really, really gets me—and this is actually something that's been stressing me out a lot lately—is at work. It's this whole thing with not finishing the very last piece of a project. 

Like, I will spend hours on a client proposal, right? I'll do all the research, pull the demographics, get the pricing tiers perfectly aligned in the spreadsheet—which takes forever, by the way, because our company's template is just incredibly clunky and outdated—and I'll get the whole document completely written and ready to go. I’ll get most of the proposal done, but then... I just leave off the last step. Like, I literally just won't send the final version to the client. It just sits there. 

Or, oh my gosh, it happens all the time with our CRM system, too. We use Salesforce, and it's an absolute beast to navigate, but I'll do all the hard work of making the calls and doing the pitch, and I'll get the CRM update mostly done, but then I'll totally fail to log the follow-up or check the final box to close out the task. And the craziest part is that I fully meant to finish it! It's not like I'm sitting there deciding to slack off or be lazy. I'll be 99 percent done, and it’s almost like my brain just goes, "Okay, we did the hard part, we're finished here," and my attention just completely shifts to the next email or the next phone call. 

And then, you know, three days later my manager will message me like, "Hey, did you ever send that deck to the Smith account?" and I'll look at my drafts folder and it's just sitting right there, completely finished, just waiting for me to hit send. It is so incredibly frustrating because I did all the heavy lifting, you know? I put in all the actual effort! I just didn't cross the finish line. So, yeah, I definitely lose focus right at the very end of things, even when I have every intention of wrapping it up properly.
Do you often act on impulse without thinking through the consequences?

Um, acting on impulse? Like, doing things without thinking about what's going to happen? No, I really don't think I do that. I mean, I know sometimes people picture advertising sales agents as these really spontaneous, fly-by-the-seat-of-their-pants types who just, you know, go rogue and make wild promises to clients just to close a deal, but I am definitely not like that. Actually, I'm probably the opposite when it comes to making decisions or taking action on things that actually matter. 

Like, just to give you an example, last week my boyfriend and I were looking at booking a vacation for our anniversary, and he was totally ready to just click "buy" on this non-refundable flight to Cabo because it was on a flash sale and he just wanted to lock it in. But I was the one who was like, "Wait, pause, we need to check the PTO calendar, we need to make sure we aren't going during hurricane season, we have to see if the resort actually has decent reviews and isn't just using wide-angle stock photos to make the pool look bigger." I literally spent three hours reading TripAdvisor reviews and cross-referencing weather patterns before I would even let him put his credit card in. 

And at work, it's the exact same way. If I'm putting together a pitch for a huge ad buy, I don't just throw numbers out there or promise deliverables without running it by the fulfillment team first. Because if you act impulsively in advertising, you end up with a furious client and a manager breathing down your neck, and I absolutely hate dealing with that kind of conflict. I overthink things way too much to just jump in blindly. I mean, sure, I might suddenly decide to get up and go get a coffee because I just need to walk, like I was saying earlier, but that's not really something that has bad consequences, you know? That's just stretching my legs. But actual impulsive actions where I don't think about the fallout or how it affects people? No, definitely not. I'm actually pretty cautious about all that stuff, probably to a fault sometimes.
Do you have trouble organizing your time or prioritizing tasks?

Oh, wow. Yes. Organizing my time and figuring out what to prioritize is... honestly, it's probably one of the biggest headaches I deal with every single day. Especially with how fast-paced ad sales is, you'd think I'd have a bulletproof system by now, but it is just a complete mess. 

Like, when I'm putting together a new campaign for a client, my notes are just everywhere. It's actually kind of embarrassing. I'll have some crucial details buried in an email thread, and then I'll have written down the client's budget constraints on a neon pink sticky note that's currently stuck to the bottom of my monitor. And then I have my actual physical planner—which I bought at Target at the beginning of the year because I thought, you know, "Oh, a nice leather-bound planner will totally fix my life and make me super organized," right? But I only write in it half the time, so half the campaign info is in there, and the rest is spread across like, forty random browser tabs I leave open on my second monitor because I'm terrified I'll forget about them if I close them. 

And because everything is so incredibly scattered like that, when I actually sit down at my desk to work, I have absolutely no idea where to begin. It's like my brain just completely short-circuits looking at the mess. So instead of just picking one thing and starting the actual work, I waste a massive amount of time just trying to figure out what to do first. I'll literally sit there for an hour just shuffling my sticky notes around, clicking back and forth between my tabs, and looking at my planner, trying to magically prioritize it all. 

I'll think, "Okay, I need to email the fulfillment team, but wait, I should check the inventory first, but wait, I need to reply to that client about the deck." And because it's not in one cohesive list, I just get completely paralyzed. It's so frustrating because I know what needs to get done, theoretically, but putting it into an actual step-by-step order? It's like trying to untangle a giant knot of delicate necklaces. You just sit there pulling at different strings and getting nowhere. By the time I finally decide what the most important task actually is, I've already lost half my morning just stressing about it. So, yeah, prioritizing and organizing is a huge, huge struggle for me.
Do you find it hard to focus on reading or other quiet activities when you're alone?

Oh, definitely. Reading is... well, it's actually a huge struggle for me, especially when it's something dense. Like, in advertising sales, we get these massive client briefs. They are just pages and pages of brand guidelines, target demographics, and historical ad spend, and I'll sit down at my desk to read through one, and I'll make sure it's totally quiet, right? Like, I'll close my office door, put my phone on silent, the whole nine yards, because I know I need to concentrate. 

And I always start out really focused! I'll get through the first section and think, "Okay, I'm doing great, I'm absorbing this." But then, literally just a few minutes later, I'll sort of... snap out of a daze, I guess? And I'll realize I have just been staring at the exact same paragraph for I don't even know how long. My eyes are physically looking at the words, but my brain is just completely elsewhere, and I will have absolutely no idea what the last point was. I'll have to go back and re-read the same sentence like three or four times just to make it stick, which makes getting through a ten-page brief take an embarrassing amount of time. 

And honestly, it happens in our longer strategy meetings, too. We have these quarterly alignment meetings that drag on forever, and even if the room is relatively quiet and someone is just presenting a deck, I'll be looking right at the screen, staring at a specific slide, and suddenly I realize I haven't processed a single thing for the last five minutes. I'll just be staring at a pie chart with zero comprehension of what it means. It's like the quietness almost makes it harder, you know? Because there's nothing active to keep my brain engaged, so it just kind of floats away, even when I'm trying really, really hard to pay attention to the material.
Do you have trouble managing your emotions when you're in a situation where you can't get up and move around?

Managing my emotions? Like, getting upset or angry just because I'm stuck in a chair? Um, no, I wouldn't really say that. I mean, don't get me wrong, I definitely get physically uncomfortable if I'm trapped somewhere for a really long time. 

Like, just last month, I had to fly out to Chicago for a big pitch with a prospective client—which was a whole ordeal in itself because the airline delayed us twice while we were already out on the tarmac—and I was stuck in a window seat with this guy completely passed out next to me. So I couldn't even get up to use the restroom or stretch my legs for literally three and a half hours. And yeah, I was definitely feeling, you know, antsy. My legs were doing that bouncy thing, and I kept shifting around in my seat, trying to find a comfortable position, just really, really wishing I could stand up and walk down the aisle for a second. 

But emotionally? I wasn't, like, having a breakdown or getting furious about it. I wasn't snapping at the flight attendant or feeling like I was going to burst into tears or anything dramatic like that. I just felt physically restless, but mentally and emotionally, I was completely fine. I just put on a movie on my iPad and dealt with it until we landed. 

And it's the same thing at work. Even in those super long quarterly alignment meetings I mentioned earlier—the ones where I completely zone out staring at the pie charts—I might be bored out of my mind and wishing I was back at my desk so I could actually get some work done, but I'm not sitting there feeling overwhelmed with emotion or unable to control my temper. I'm actually pretty even-keeled emotionally, even when I'm physically feeling a bit trapped in a conference room. So, yeah, I don't think I have any emotional issues with that kind of stuff, just the physical urge to move, which I just kind of push through anyway.
Do you have trouble managing your emotions in your daily life?

Um, no, not really. I actually think I'm pretty stable in that department. I mean, daily life for me is mostly work, and like I was saying, ad sales is a total pressure cooker. If you can't keep your emotions in check, you're basically going to get eaten alive by the clients or the agency reps. 

Like, just to give you an idea of what I deal with... last Tuesday, we had this massive crisis with one of our biggest accounts. The client's marketing director emailed us at, I kid you not, 4:45 PM, basically threatening to pull a fifty-thousand-dollar ad buy that was supposed to launch on Wednesday morning, all because she suddenly decided she didn't like the color grading on the digital banners. And my boss was absolutely losing his mind, pacing around the office, practically hyperventilating, and our internal creative team was furious because they'd already gotten formal sign-off on those exact colors two weeks prior. 

But me? I was completely fine. I mean, I was definitely stressed because of the sheer amount of logistical workload it was about to create for me—which, you know, adding more last-minute tasks to my already disorganized mess of sticky notes and planner pages is never fun—but emotionally? I didn't yell, I didn't cry, I didn't panic. I just sat there, drafted a very polite, very diplomatic email to smooth things over with the client, and got everyone on a quick conference call to sort it out without losing the account. 

So, yeah, even when things are incredibly high-stakes or chaotic, I don't really have emotional outbursts or mood swings or anything like that in my day-to-day life. I might get frustrated with my own brain sometimes when I can't focus or figure out where to start my work, like I was talking about earlier, but as far as just general emotional management goes? I'd say I'm actually the calm one in my office most of the time. I just sort of roll with the punches, you know? I've never really been the type to fly off the handle or let my feelings get the better of me, even when maybe I have a totally valid reason to be upset about something.
Do you have trouble keeping your emotions in check when you're in a situation where things aren't going as planned?

Honestly? No, not really. I'm actually kind of the opposite when things go off the rails. I don't get emotional or lose my temper at all. 

Like... okay, just to give you another example from work, since that's where things usually go wrong for me. We had this huge client dinner planned last month at this incredibly exclusive steakhouse downtown—like, the kind of place where you have to book literally three months in advance and put down a non-refundable deposit just to hold a table for six people. I had everything planned down to the minute, the wine was pre-selected, everything. 

But then, at like 5:00 PM, while I'm literally in the back of an Uber on the way there, sitting in absolute bumper-to-bumper rush hour traffic, in the pouring rain... the restaurant calls me. They had a pipe burst in their kitchen and had to close for the night. Reservation completely canceled, zero notice. And my junior associate, who was riding in the Uber with me, started totally panicking. I mean, she was practically in tears, hyperventilating, going on and on about how we were going to lose the account and how our boss was going to fire us. 

But me? I didn't even feel my heart rate go up. I didn't get mad at the restaurant manager on the phone, I didn't snap at my associate for freaking out, I didn't cry. I just... I don't know, I just shifted into problem-solving mode. I pulled up my contacts, called a guy I know who manages a really nice upscale Italian place a few blocks away, managed to sweet-talk him into giving us their private back room on zero notice, and then I just calmly texted the clients to let them know we had a 'surprise venue change' to give them a more exclusive dining experience. I spun it completely as a positive. 

So, yeah, when plans completely fall apart, I don't get emotional at all. If anything, I get weirdly calm. I just kind of accept that the original plan is dead and focus entirely on fixing it. I've just never been the kind of person who falls apart or gets angry when the schedule gets thrown out the window, even if it's massively inconvenient and stressful. I just sort of pivot and handle it without making a fuss.
Do you often find yourself talking more than others in social situations?

Oh, wow, yeah. Um, if you asked anyone in my office, they would probably start laughing and say absolutely, yes. I am definitely a talker. 

It happens a lot, especially at work. Like, when we're doing these big team pitches? You know, the ones where we have the whole committee in the room—the account managers, the creative directors, the media buyers, everybody sitting around one of those massive mahogany conference tables. I just get really, really into it. Like, if I'm presenting a campaign idea that I actually believe in, I just sort of take off and I can't really hit the brakes. 

For example, we were pitching this huge digital rebrand for a boutique hotel chain a couple of weeks ago—which was a really cool project, they wanted to completely revamp their aesthetic to appeal to a younger, more affluent demographic, so we had all these moody, cinematic mock-ups—and I was supposed to just briefly introduce the core concept before handing it over to the media team. But I just started talking about the campaign idea, the visuals, the target audience, how we were going to integrate these specific lifestyle influencers... and I just kept going. 

And the funny thing is, while I'm doing it, I can actually hear myself going on way too long about the campaign idea. It's almost like this weird out-of-body experience where part of my brain is going, "Okay, you've made your point, wrap it up, let someone else talk," but my mouth just keeps moving because I want to make sure they understand every single nuance of the vision and I don't want to leave any dead air. 

And then, finally, I'll run out of breath and stop, and I look around the table, and... yeah. I can completely tell that other people on my team were just sitting there, waiting for a chance to speak. Like, my co-presenter will literally have her mouth half-open and her hand hovering over her notes, just waiting for a millisecond of silence so she can finally jump in and do her slide on the budget allocation. It's not that I mean to hog the spotlight or anything, I just get so wrapped up in explaining the concept that I completely steamroll the agenda. So, yeah, I definitely have a tendency to dominate the floor once I get going.
Do you often interrupt others when they're speaking?

Oh, yeah. Yeah, I definitely do that, too. I guess it kind of goes hand-in-hand with the talking too much thing I was just mentioning. It’s like... well, in our office, we have this very collaborative, open-concept layout, which is great for brainstorming, but it also means I can see what everyone is doing all the time, or I'm always walking past people's desks on my way to the kitchen. 

And if I’m just going about my day and I suddenly think of an idea while someone else is working through a deck—like, say they’re putting together the slide sequence for a big client presentation and I suddenly realize we should completely swap the order of the demographic data or use a different font for the headers—I’ll just immediately pop over to their desk. 

And the thing is, I’ll just jump right in. I’ll interrupt whatever they’re doing, or even if they’re literally in the middle of a conversation with another co-worker about something completely unrelated, I’ll just step right in and add my thought. It’s like the idea is burning a hole in my brain and I just have to get it out right then and there before it evaporates. 

And, you know, I always realize right after I do it that it probably could have waited. Like, I could have easily just sent a quick Slack message, or written it down on one of my fifty million sticky notes and brought it up at the actual review meeting later that afternoon. But in the moment, it just feels so incredibly urgent, like they absolutely need to know this one specific thought right this second before they finish the deck, or else the whole pitch is going to be ruined. So, yeah, I definitely cut people off or jump into their conversations a lot more than I probably should. I don't do it to be rude, I just get so excited about the ideas, you know?
Do you often struggle to complete tasks or projects due to difficulty sustaining focus?

Oh, absolutely. Yeah, that is probably one of my biggest hurdles at work right now. It’s actually incredibly frustrating, because in ad sales, there is just so much administrative follow-through required, you know? It’s not just the fun, glamorous pitching part that I was talking about earlier, it's all the backend paperwork and tracking. 

And it’s not that I don't do the work. That's the weird part. I’ll actually get most of a proposal or a CRM update completely done. Like, say it's Friday afternoon and I'm supposed to be doing my pipeline maintenance. I will go into the system, I’ll update the client’s new budget numbers, I’ll type out all these detailed notes from our lunch meeting, I’ll attach the new media kit... and then I just leave off the very last step. I'll just completely fail to log the actual follow-up date, or I'll just leave the window open and forget to hit save. 

Or with proposals! Oh my gosh, this happens all the time. I will spend three entire days drafting this beautiful, comprehensive quarterly proposal for a client. I’ll get the pricing tiers perfect, I'll map out the entire campaign timeline, I'll even proofread the whole thing twice. But then... I just don't send it. It’s like my brain just decides, "Okay, the hard part is over, we figured it out, we're done here," and completely checks out right before the finish line. 

I fully mean to finish it, too! I really do. Half the time I even have the email drafted to the client with the PDF attached, but then the phone will ring, or I'll tab over to check an inventory spreadsheet, and that draft will just sit in my outbox for three days. And then my director will casually ask if we've heard back from the client yet, and I have to do this whole internal panic where I'm like, "Oh, let me check on that," while frantically tabbing over to my email to finally hit send on the final version. It's just so annoying because I do ninety-nine percent of the heavy lifting, but because I miss that one tiny final step, it basically looks like I didn't do the work at all. So, yeah, sustaining focus all the way to the literal end of a project is definitely a huge struggle.
Do you often find yourself saying things without thinking them through?

Oh, wow. Yes. Um, that is actually a huge thing for me, and it's honestly so embarrassing when it happens. 

Because in ad sales, you know, you really want to project this image of being totally on the ball, like you have all the data right at your fingertips and you're always one step ahead. So when we're in a meeting... well, like, just last Tuesday, for example. We had this massive quarterly review with one of our biggest accounts—they do all these direct-to-consumer wellness products, really cool brand—and their marketing director was going over the analytics for the latest social push we did for them. 

And she started asking a question, something like, "So, looking at the click-through rates for the Instagram stories..." and my brain immediately just filled in the rest of the blank. I assumed she was going to ask why the conversion rate dipped over the weekend, because I had literally just been analyzing that exact metric that morning and I was already feeling a little defensive about it. 

So I just completely jumped in. I didn't even let her finish the sentence. I just blurted out this whole long explanation about the algorithm changes and weekend user habits and how we were already pivoting the strategy to compensate. And she just looked at me, kind of blinked, and was like, "Actually, I was going to ask if we could increase the budget for those stories because the overall engagement is so high." 

I wanted to melt into the floor. It happens all the time—I often jump in with an answer before a client or coworker has finished asking the question, and then I realize I answered the wrong thing or cut them off entirely. 

It happens with my internal team, too. My manager will start asking me about a project timeline, and I'll just blurt out an answer about the budget, and then he has to awkwardly back up and tell me that wasn't what he was asking. It's like my mouth is moving five seconds ahead of my actual listening comprehension. I just get so eager to respond, or my brain assumes I know exactly where they're going with it, that I just throw an answer out there without actually taking a breath to think it through or hear them out. I really struggle to just sit there and let people finish their thought.
Do you often find yourself making careless mistakes or overlooking details in your work or daily activities?

Actually, no. That’s one thing I don’t really do, which is kind of ironic, I guess, given the whole "forgetting to hit send" thing I was just talking about. But the actual work itself? The details? No, I’m actually incredibly meticulous about that. 

In ad sales, if you mess up a CPM or quote the wrong inventory availability, it can literally cost the agency thousands of dollars, and it makes you look totally incompetent to the client. So I am hyper-aware of the details. I mean, I will sit there and go over a pitch deck three or four times before I even think about wrapping it up. I’ll check the fonts, I’ll check the slide alignment, I’ll recalculate the media spend in my head and then on a calculator just to be absolutely one hundred percent sure the math adds up. 

It’s almost like I over-focus on the details, you know? Like, I rarely ever have a typo or a wrong number in my spreadsheets. My manager actually praises my accuracy a lot, which is nice. I'm usually the one catching little things that other people miss. Like, just last week, one of the junior reps put together a mock-up and used a client's old logo—the one from like, two rebrands ago—and I spotted it instantly from across the table. 

So the quality of the work is always really, really solid. It’s just... getting that perfectly accurate, beautifully detailed document out the door that’s the problem. But the details themselves? No, I really don't overlook those. I wouldn't say I make careless mistakes at all. I'm pretty locked in when it comes to getting the actual facts and figures right.
Have you ever been diagnosed with Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder or do you think you might have it?

Um, no. No, I haven't ever been officially diagnosed with anything like that. I mean, it's not something that was ever really brought up when I was a kid, you know? Like, I did fine in school, I got my degree, I've always managed to hold down a job. So it just wasn't on the radar. 

But, like... do I think I might have it? I don't know. Honestly, that's kind of why I'm here. Because lately, it just feels like everything is so much harder than it needs to be, or harder than it seems to be for other people in my office. Like, I look around at my coworkers, and they just sit down, do the work, send the email, and move on. And for me, it's this whole dramatic saga of starting, stopping, getting distracted, panicking, interrupting people... 

And I've started seeing all these videos online, you know, like on TikTok or whatever, where people talk about their experiences, and I'm like, "Wait, that's exactly what I do." Like the whole thing with getting 99% done with a project and just completely abandoning ship? I thought that was just a weird personality quirk I had, but apparently, it's a whole thing. 

So, I don't know for sure. I'm not trying to, like, self-diagnose off of social media or anything, because I know that's a terrible idea, but... yeah, it's definitely crossed my mind that maybe there's an actual reason why my brain works this way. It would honestly be a bit of a relief if there was a reason, instead of just me being somehow broken or lazy, even though I know I'm not lazy because I work so hard. But yeah, no official diagnosis ever. Just a lot of wondering lately.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has difficulty with self-regulation of emotions in specific contexts
doctor.question: Do you have trouble keeping your emotions in check when you're in a situation where things aren't going as planned?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about emotional dysregulation or frustration tolerance when things do not go as planned, which is not covered by my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Honestly? No, not really. I'm actually kind of the opposite when things go off the rails. I don't get emotional or lose my temper at all. 

Like... okay, just to give you another example from work, since that's where things usually go wrong for me. We had this huge client dinner planned last month at this incredibly exclusive steakhouse downtown—like, the kind of place where you have to book literally three months in advance and put down a non-refundable deposit just to hold a table for six people. I had everything planned down to the minute, the wine was pre-selected, everything. 

But then, at like 5:00 PM, while I'm literally in the back of an Uber on the way there, sitting in absolute bumper-to-bumper rush hour traffic, in the pouring rain... the restaurant calls me. They had a pipe burst in their kitchen and had to close for the night. Reservation completely canceled, zero notice. And my junior associate, who was riding in the Uber with me, started totally panicking. I mean, she was practically in tears, hyperventilating, going on and on about how we were going to lose the account and how our boss was going to fire us. 

But me? I didn't even feel my heart rate go up. I didn't get mad at the restaurant manager on the phone, I didn't snap at my associate for freaking out, I didn't cry. I just... I don't know, I just shifted into problem-solving mode. I pulled up my contacts, called a guy I know who manages a really nice upscale Italian place a few blocks away, managed to sweet-talk him into giving us their private back room on zero notice, and then I just calmly texted the clients to let them know we had a 'surprise venue change' to give them a more exclusive dining experience. I spun it completely as a positive. 

So, yeah, when plans completely fall apart, I don't get emotional at all. If anything, I get weirdly calm. I just kind of accept that the original plan is dead and focus entirely on fixing it. I've just never been the kind of person who falls apart or gets angry when the schedule gets thrown out the window, even if it's massively inconvenient and stressful. I just sort of pivot and handle it without making a fuss.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences excessive talkativeness
doctor.question: Do you often find yourself talking more than others in social situations?

target_item.name: Excessive_Talking
target_item.manifestation: In team pitches I can hear myself going on too long about the campaign idea, and by the time I stop, I can tell other people were waiting for a chance to speak.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if I talk more than others in social situations, which directly aligns with the symptom of excessive talking.

patient.answer:
Oh, wow, yeah. Um, if you asked anyone in my office, they would probably start laughing and say absolutely, yes. I am definitely a talker. 

It happens a lot, especially at work. Like, when we're doing these big team pitches? You know, the ones where we have the whole committee in the room—the account managers, the creative directors, the media buyers, everybody sitting around one of those massive mahogany conference tables. I just get really, really into it. Like, if I'm presenting a campaign idea that I actually believe in, I just sort of take off and I can't really hit the brakes. 

For example, we were pitching this huge digital rebrand for a boutique hotel chain a couple of weeks ago—which was a really cool project, they wanted to completely revamp their aesthetic to appeal to a younger, more affluent demographic, so we had all these moody, cinematic mock-ups—and I was supposed to just briefly introduce the core concept before handing it over to the media team. But I just started talking about the campaign idea, the visuals, the target audience, how we were going to integrate these specific lifestyle influencers... and I just kept going. 

And the funny thing is, while I'm doing it, I can actually hear myself going on way too long about the campaign idea. It's almost like this weird out-of-body experience where part of my brain is going, "Okay, you've made your point, wrap it up, let someone else talk," but my mouth just keeps moving because I want to make sure they understand every single nuance of the vision and I don't want to leave any dead air. 

And then, finally, I'll run out of breath and stop, and I look around the table, and... yeah. I can completely tell that other people on my team were just sitting there, waiting for a chance to speak. Like, my co-presenter will literally have her mouth half-open and her hand hovering over her notes, just waiting for a millisecond of silence so she can finally jump in and do her slide on the budget allocation. It's not that I mean to hog the spotlight or anything, I just get so wrapped up in explaining the concept that I completely steamroll the agenda. So, yeah, I definitely have a tendency to dominate the floor once I get going.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has difficulty with self-control in social situations
doctor.question: Do you often interrupt others when they're speaking?

patient.answer:
Oh, yeah. Yeah, I definitely do that, too. I guess it kind of goes hand-in-hand with the talking too much thing I was just mentioning. It’s like... well, in our office, we have this very collaborative, open-concept layout, which is great for brainstorming, but it also means I can see what everyone is doing all the time, or I'm always walking past people's desks on my way to the kitchen. 

And if I’m just going about my day and I suddenly think of an idea while someone else is working through a deck—like, say they’re putting together the slide sequence for a big client presentation and I suddenly realize we should completely swap the order of the demographic data or use a different font for the headers—I’ll just immediately pop over to their desk. 

And the thing is, I’ll just jump right in. I’ll interrupt whatever they’re doing, or even if they’re literally in the middle of a conversation with another co-worker about something completely unrelated, I’ll just step right in and add my thought. It’s like the idea is burning a hole in my brain and I just have to get it out right then and there before it evaporates. 

And, you know, I always realize right after I do it that it probably could have waited. Like, I could have easily just sent a quick Slack message, or written it down on one of my fifty million sticky notes and brought it up at the actual review meeting later that afternoon. But in the moment, it just feels so incredibly urgent, like they absolutely need to know this one specific thought right this second before they finish the deck, or else the whole pitch is going to be ruined. So, yeah, I definitely cut people off or jump into their conversations a lot more than I probably should. I don't do it to be rude, I just get so excited about the ideas, you know?

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's symptoms are consistent with Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD), specifically the predominance of inattentive symptoms
doctor.question: Do you often struggle to complete tasks or projects due to difficulty sustaining focus?

target_item.name: Instruction_Follow through_Difficulty
target_item.manifestation: I’ll get most of a proposal or CRM update done, but then I leave off the last step, like sending the final version or logging the follow-up, even though I meant to finish it.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about struggling to complete tasks and projects, which directly corresponds to failing to finish duties or follow through on tasks.

patient.answer:
Oh, absolutely. Yeah, that is probably one of my biggest hurdles at work right now. It’s actually incredibly frustrating, because in ad sales, there is just so much administrative follow-through required, you know? It’s not just the fun, glamorous pitching part that I was talking about earlier, it's all the backend paperwork and tracking. 

And it’s not that I don't do the work. That's the weird part. I’ll actually get most of a proposal or a CRM update completely done. Like, say it's Friday afternoon and I'm supposed to be doing my pipeline maintenance. I will go into the system, I’ll update the client’s new budget numbers, I’ll type out all these detailed notes from our lunch meeting, I’ll attach the new media kit... and then I just leave off the very last step. I'll just completely fail to log the actual follow-up date, or I'll just leave the window open and forget to hit save. 

Or with proposals! Oh my gosh, this happens all the time. I will spend three entire days drafting this beautiful, comprehensive quarterly proposal for a client. I’ll get the pricing tiers perfect, I'll map out the entire campaign timeline, I'll even proofread the whole thing twice. But then... I just don't send it. It’s like my brain just decides, "Okay, the hard part is over, we figured it out, we're done here," and completely checks out right before the finish line. 

I fully mean to finish it, too! I really do. Half the time I even have the email drafted to the client with the PDF attached, but then the phone will ring, or I'll tab over to check an inventory spreadsheet, and that draft will just sit in my outbox for three days. And then my director will casually ask if we've heard back from the client yet, and I have to do this whole internal panic where I'm like, "Oh, let me check on that," while frantically tabbing over to my email to finally hit send on the final version. It's just so annoying because I do ninety-nine percent of the heavy lifting, but because I miss that one tiny final step, it basically looks like I didn't do the work at all. So, yeah, sustaining focus all the way to the literal end of a project is definitely a huge struggle.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has difficulty with self-control of speech
doctor.question: Do you often find yourself saying things without thinking them through?

target_item.name: Blurting_Answers
target_item.manifestation: I often jump in with an answer before a client or coworker has finished asking the question, and then I realize I answered the wrong thing or cut them off.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about impulsivity in speech, which maps to blurting out answers before a question has been completed.

patient.answer:
Oh, wow. Yes. Um, that is actually a huge thing for me, and it's honestly so embarrassing when it happens. 

Because in ad sales, you know, you really want to project this image of being totally on the ball, like you have all the data right at your fingertips and you're always one step ahead. So when we're in a meeting... well, like, just last Tuesday, for example. We had this massive quarterly review with one of our biggest accounts—they do all these direct-to-consumer wellness products, really cool brand—and their marketing director was going over the analytics for the latest social push we did for them. 

And she started asking a question, something like, "So, looking at the click-through rates for the Instagram stories..." and my brain immediately just filled in the rest of the blank. I assumed she was going to ask why the conversion rate dipped over the weekend, because I had literally just been analyzing that exact metric that morning and I was already feeling a little defensive about it. 

So I just completely jumped in. I didn't even let her finish the sentence. I just blurted out this whole long explanation about the algorithm changes and weekend user habits and how we were already pivoting the strategy to compensate. And she just looked at me, kind of blinked, and was like, "Actually, I was going to ask if we could increase the budget for those stories because the overall engagement is so high." 

I wanted to melt into the floor. It happens all the time—I often jump in with an answer before a client or coworker has finished asking the question, and then I realize I answered the wrong thing or cut them off entirely. 

It happens with my internal team, too. My manager will start asking me about a project timeline, and I'll just blurt out an answer about the budget, and then he has to awkwardly back up and tell me that wasn't what he was asking. It's like my mouth is moving five seconds ahead of my actual listening comprehension. I just get so eager to respond, or my brain assumes I know exactly where they're going with it, that I just throw an answer out there without actually taking a breath to think it through or hear them out. I really struggle to just sit there and let people finish their thought.

patient.answer:
Actually, no. That’s one thing I don’t really do, which is kind of ironic, I guess, given the whole "forgetting to hit send" thing I was just talking about. But the actual work itself? The details? No, I’m actually incredibly meticulous about that. 

In ad sales, if you mess up a CPM or quote the wrong inventory availability, it can literally cost the agency thousands of dollars, and it makes you look totally incompetent to the client. So I am hyper-aware of the details. I mean, I will sit there and go over a pitch deck three or four times before I even think about wrapping it up. I’ll check the fonts, I’ll check the slide alignment, I’ll recalculate the media spend in my head and then on a calculator just to be absolutely one hundred percent sure the math adds up. 

It’s almost like I over-focus on the details, you know? Like, I rarely ever have a typo or a wrong number in my spreadsheets. My manager actually praises my accuracy a lot, which is nice. I'm usually the one catching little things that other people miss. Like, just last week, one of the junior reps put together a mock-up and used a client's old logo—the one from like, two rebrands ago—and I spotted it instantly from across the table. 

So the quality of the work is always really, really solid. It’s just... getting that perfectly accurate, beautifully detailed document out the door that’s the problem. But the details themselves? No, I really don't overlook those. I wouldn't say I make careless mistakes at all. I'm pretty locked in when it comes to getting the actual facts and figures right.

Um, no. No, I haven't ever been officially diagnosed with anything like that. I mean, it's not something that was ever really brought up when I was a kid, you know? Like, I did fine in school, I got my degree, I've always managed to hold down a job. So it just wasn't on the radar. 

But, like... do I think I might have it? I don't know. Honestly, that's kind of why I'm here. Because lately, it just feels like everything is so much harder than it needs to be, or harder than it seems to be for other people in my office. Like, I look around at my coworkers, and they just sit down, do the work, send the email, and move on. And for me, it's this whole dramatic saga of starting, stopping, getting distracted, panicking, interrupting people... 

And I've started seeing all these videos online, you know, like on TikTok or whatever, where people talk about their experiences, and I'm like, "Wait, that's exactly what I do." Like the whole thing with getting 99% done with a project and just completely abandoning ship? I thought that was just a weird personality quirk I had, but apparently, it's a whole thing. 

So, I don't know for sure. I'm not trying to, like, self-diagnose off of social media or anything, because I know that's a terrible idea, but... yeah, it's definitely crossed my mind that maybe there's an actual reason why my brain works this way. It would honestly be a bit of a relief if there was a reason, instead of just me being somehow broken or lazy, even though I know I'm not lazy because I work so hard. But yeah, no official diagnosis ever. Just a lot of wondering lately.
